item.title: Key role of services trade highlighted
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Key role of services trade highlighted Services: Increasing demand seen for high-quality imports China will further open its services sector, ease market access and expand imports of high-quality services as it seeks to create new growth drivers for trade in services and share the opportunities of its vast market with the world, government officials said on Wednesday. Speaking at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services in Beijing on Wednesday, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang said China will further refine the negative list for cross-border trade in services, widen market access in the services sector and foster a more favorable business environment. Ding, who is also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said the nation will accelerate the development of new business forms and models such as digital services trade, develop knowledge-intensive services and expand exports of producer services. The 2026 CIFTIS, which runs through Sunday, has drawn participants from 90 countries, regions and international organizations. More than 1,800 companies, including Honeywell, McDonald's and Schneider Electric, are exhibiting on-site. More than 100 new products and services will make their debut at the fair, covering fields such as information and communications, financial technology, and digital and intelligent healthcare. Against a backdrop of growing uncertainty in the global trading system, officials from international organizations and foreign governments said during the fair's opening ceremony that services are set to play an increasingly important role in global trade and supply chains. Johanna Hill, deputy director-general of the World Trade Organization, said services are becoming an increasingly important part of global supply chains, supporting not only production but also design, management, logistics and distribution. She said China can contribute to global services trade by demonstrating the benefits of more competitive services markets and sharing its experience with developing economies. Highlighting the opportunities for developing economies, Constantino Chiwenga, the Zimbabwean vice-president, said automation and digital innovation are reshaping the global economy and creating new opportunities for trade in services. Zimbabwe is seeking deeper services cooperation with China through investment, technology transfer and skills development in areas including healthcare, financial services, transportation and professional services, he said. Alexander Poulev, Bulgaria's deputy prime minister and minister of economy, investments and industry, said trade in services is a key pillar of Bulgaria-China economic ties, with the country seeking stronger long-term partnerships with Chinese businesses. "Stronger investment cooperation could create new supply chains and add greater value to bilateral trade," Poulev said. Policy push Advancing the high-quality development of services trade is a key task outlined in China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), which calls for intensified efforts to optimize negative list management of services trade, ease cross-border restrictions, encourage services exports and foster knowledge-intensive services trade. Digitalization and emerging technologies are expected to play an increasingly important role in reshaping the services sector and expanding cross-border trade. Yin Li, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Beijing Municipal Committee, said Beijing stands ready to work with global partners to facilitate trade flows, expand services trade and share the opportunities of China's vast market. China's trade in services totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan ($663 billion) in the first seven months of this year, up 8.3 percent year-on-year, data from the Ministry of Commerce showed. The expansion of services trade is also translating into new opportunities for companies across a range of sectors. James Evans, general manager of Cathay Cargo, a business unit of the Hong Kong-based Cathay Group, said the company sees the Chinese mainland's continued industrial upgrading, expanding global trade links and increasingly diversified import demand as important drivers. "On the import side, temperature-controlled cargo is performing particularly well," Evans said. "We are seeing increasing demand for the transportation of fresh produce and pharmaceuticals into the Chinese mainland, reflecting rising consumer demand for high-quality imported goods and the growing importance of reliable cold-chain logistics." State-owned Shenyang Northern Aircraft Maintenance and Engineering Co in Shenyang, Liaoning province, handled 46 million yuan worth of imports and exports between January and August under the bonded maintenance model, a customs arrangement that allows companies to import faulty or damaged foreign-made products without paying import duties, provided they are repaired and then reexported. Five auxiliary power units, or APUs, were repaired and delivered during the period, according to Shenyang Customs. Wang Lulu, the company's president, said the company will seek more orders from foreign airlines and expand high-end producer services, including APU testing, maintenance and overhaul, particularly in Central and Southeast Asia.

item.title: UN General Assembly starts 81st session
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
UN General Assembly starts 81st session The United Nations General Assembly opened its 81st session on Tuesday at the organization's New York headquarters with the theme of "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All". Khalilur Rahman, president of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, or UNGA, said his main pledge for the session was to "work tirelessly to revive trust in this institution, upon which success of our collective action ultimately depends". In his opening remarks, Rahman said the UN has "often fallen short of the expectations placed upon it" as conflicts continue to cause immense human suffering, development gains remain "feeble and fragile", and climate impacts intensify. "Together, these challenges have brought trust in multilateralism under tremendous strain," he said. "A widening trust deficit is testing confidence in international institutions and collective action – a deficit that we must close by working together through dialogue, renewed cooperation, and delivery." Rahman, who is also Bangladesh foreign minister, said the assembly would focus its work during the coming year on six priorities: strengthening peace and security, accelerating sustainable development, advancing climate action, promoting human rights, ensuring technological transformation serves people everywhere, and restoring trust in multilateralism. "Today, our responsibility is not merely to defend this institution – there are good reasons to do so – but to strengthen it; not simply to invoke the trust on which multilateralism depends, but to earn it every day," Rahman said. On the selection of the next secretary-general, Rahman said he will "ensure this process remains fair, inclusive, and transparent", noting that the secretary-general will be appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council. He also urged all member states to pay their assessed contributions "in full, on time, and without conditions", while stressing that the UN itself must be held accountable for how it uses its resources. "We have a solemn duty to ensure that every single resource – every penny – is used responsibly, transparently, and effectively," Rahman said. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said Tuesday's opening marked the last time he will attend the start of a General Assembly session as UN secretary-general. "But as I join you in this opening of a General Assembly session for the last time as secretary-general, I have enormous hope thanks to the work that happens here," he said. "From the start, this has been the place where the world's toughest and most consequential problems are confronted head-on." He warned that the international system is confronting conflicts, divisions, and the risk of nuclear escalation, alongside persistent poverty and inequality, worsening climate change, displacement, and slow progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. "Human suffering is intensifying while funding for aid and development is being slashed," he said. "The institutions of the multilateral system, from the UN Security Council to the international financial architecture, are straining to meet the moment. "International law and human rights, the core of our organization, are too often flouted with impunity. And geopolitical mistrust and suspicion continue to block the effective solutions we need and erode people's faith in the possibilities of global cooperation." The opening of the 81st session followed the closing of the 80th session of the General Assembly, which was presided over by Annalena Baerbock. In her closing remarks on Tuesday, Baerbock said the previous session had underscored the urgency of reforming the United Nations. "This 80th session also made clear that without deep reform, this organization will not last," she said. Baerbock also said the selection of the next secretary-general, a process that will continue during the 81st session, is a major test for the institution. "The decision the Security Council and the General Assembly will take in the 81st session will define if the UN practices what it preaches," she said. "Indeed, it might be the credibility test of this institution for this decade."

item.title: Digital tech helps drive travel industry growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Digital tech helps drive travel industry growth 'China Bound·Beijing' smart English cultural tourism platform launched While digital technologies are reshaping the tourism industry and making travel more efficient and accessible, they can also foster human connections and cooperation, and safeguard communities and culture to drive tourism growth, participants at a cultural and tourism event said on Wednesday. They made the remarks during the opening ceremony of the World Conference on Tourism Cooperation and Development 2026 in Beijing's Shougang Park. Hosted by the World Tourism Cities Federation, or WTCF, and co-organized by the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism, the conference attracted representatives of the WTCF's member cities, heads of international organizations, cross-border travel traders, diplomatic envoys to China and experts from more than 50 countries and regions. Themed "Smart Tourism, Shared Prosperity", the conference runs through Friday and is being held amid the ongoing 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services. "Our responsibility is not to choose between residents and visitors, but to build a model in which both can thrive. Smart tourism gives us practical tools to achieve this balance. For example, digital platforms can improve accessibility, multilingual information and journey planning," said Olaf McKay, mayor of Valletta, the capital of Malta. He added that China's visa-free policy is making the country more accessible for Maltese citizens, especially young people and students, enabling them to experience China's traditions and culture firsthand. Ben Montgomery, vice-chairwoman of the Pacific Asia Travel Association, a not-for-profit membership association headquartered in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, agreed. "Artificial intelligence, data analytics and digital platforms are reshaping how people discover, book and experience destinations worldwide. As we embrace these tools, we must remember a fundamental truth: Tourism is ultimately about people," she said. She added that the true value of the tourism industry lies in human connection — by linking visitors with local communities, bridging cultures and fostering shared understanding across borders. "Beijing is a city where centuries of rich history seamlessly meet modern innovation. … Today is about turning ideas into practical collaborations through partnerships, matchmaking and open exchanges," Montgomery said. Dai Bin, director of the China Tourism Academy, noted that tourism allows international visitors to get close to authentic daily life in China and try out Chinese services. He said that Beijing has rolled out a number of AI-backed, visitor-friendly initiatives, such as cross-regional tax refunds, providing a referable model for AI-driven cultural and tourism applications. Joseph Daniel Lema, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, the United States, unveiled the World Tourism Cities Development Report (2025-26) by the WTCF at the event. The report examines the opportunities and challenges in safety governance, technology adoption, industrial integration, cultural heritage, brand building and regional coordination, and offers forward-looking and actionable policy recommendations. The top 10 cities in the World Tourism Cities Development Comprehensive Ranking are New York, Tokyo, Paris, London, Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Milan, Istanbul and Dubai. "Beijing has moved up its ranking, reflecting the strength of cultural resources, smart governance and safety assurance," Lema said. One-stop gateway At the conference, China Daily and the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism jointly launched the "China Bound·Beijing" English cultural tourism platform, offering international visitors a new one-stop gateway to explore Beijing. The smart platform includes an English-language website (chinabound.cn/beijing), as well as dedicated pages on the Alipay and WeChat mini-programs of China Bound. It provides services ranging from itinerary planning to AI-powered assistance, enabling overseas travelers to experience the unique beauty of Beijing. "We aim to tell Beijing's cultural-tourism stories in a language overseas audiences understand, and translate the city's resource advantages into inbound tourism appeal. We promote immersive experiences such as intangible cultural heritage to enable inbound visitors to stay longer for in-depth travel," said Zheng Fang, deputy director of the Beijing Municipal Bureau of Culture and Tourism. xulin@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Beijing Confucius Temple
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Beijing Confucius Temple was built during the Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368) and served as a national site for ceremonies honoring Confucius throughout the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties (1271-1911). It stands alongside the Imperial College, the highest institution of learning in imperial China at the time. Its courtyards are arranged along a central axis, with ancient cypress trees and rows of stone steles, and centered on the solemn Dacheng Hall, where Confucius was honored. On Teachers' Day, step into this historic complex, pause before the statue of Confucius as a teacher outside Dacheng Gate, and discover a tradition of respecting teachers and valuing learning that has endured in China for centuries. www.chinabound.cn Travel with ease in China, and with meaning.

item.title: Tiangong class inspires Hong Kong, Macao students
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-10
Tiangong class inspires Hong Kong, Macao students A live-broadcast class given on Wednesday by the in-orbit Shenzhou XXIII crew, including Lai Ka-ying, the first astronaut from Hong Kong to travel into space, ignited a passion among students in the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions for exploring space and inspired them to contribute to national aerospace exploration in the future. The 90-minute class, a special session for Hong Kong and Macao students under the Tiangong Class series, was beamed from China's Tiangong space station to the students starting at 9:50 am local time. Three astronauts — Lai, the mission's payload specialist, commander Zhu Yangzhu and pilot Zhang Zhiyuan — shared their knowledge and experiences with the students. They demonstrated several phenomena in a zero-gravity environment, including using a towel-covered table tennis paddle to strike a water droplet, which bounced off the towel just like a ping-pong ball. The astronauts also explained the space station's living facilities and food supplies. Education authorities in Hong Kong and Macao encouraged all local primary and secondary schools to arrange for students and teachers to watch the broadcast from their own classrooms. Students at Lai's alma mater, Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College, watched the class in a specially designated space, and were joined by 60 students and educators from 15 Macao schools. Addressing the audience gathered at the school, Hong Kong SAR Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the class gave Hong Kong and Macao students the opportunity to interact with astronauts aboard Tiangong and to appreciate the nation's aerospace achievements and ambitions. Lee said that Lai, who was born and raised in Hong Kong, has shown that the space dream is never out of reach. Hong Kong people can also contribute to the nation's aerospace endeavors, he said, adding that scientists in Hong Kong have provided equipment and technical support for the country's lunar, Martian and other space exploration missions. Eight students — six from Hong Kong and two from Macao — asked the three astronauts questions during the real-time dialogue session. A Hong Kong primary school student asked what kind of preparations astronauts make before a spacewalk and what psychological and physiological experiences they undergo during extravehicular activities. Zhu said the crewmembers rehearse with equipment, conduct drills, examine spacesuits and monitor their physical condition before a spacewalk. Although spacewalks are physically grueling, he added, looking out into space gives the astronauts a real sense of what exploring the universe is all about. Doris Cheong Weng-man, from Macao's Sacred Heart Canossian College, English Section, asked what the astronauts considered to be the most profound challenges they faced during training. Lai said the most memorable ones included desert survival training, sleep deprivation training and a six-day cave training session. "The training posed significant physical and psychological challenges, and made me realize the importance of discipline and teamwork," she added. At Pui Kiu Middle School in Hong Kong, more than 100 students gathered to watch the class. In 2003, China's first in-orbit astronaut, Yang Liwei, planted an oak tree at the school during his visit to the Hong Kong SAR. Kwan See-heng, a 10th-grade student, said that this was the first time he had witnessed a class presented via a live question-and-answer session. "As a student of science, I hope to get involved in scientific research and development, and to contribute to space technologies if given the chance," Kwan said. William Xu, Li Xiang and Flora Ni contributed to this story. atlasshao@chinadailyhk.com

item.title: Evacuated residents returning home after Gyirong mudslide
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-09
Evacuated residents returning home after mudslide hits border port in China's Xizang GYIRONG, Xizang -- A total of 444 residents evacuated from nearby villages in Gyirong town, Southwest China's Xizang autonomous region, have safely returned home after the threat from a barrier lake was largely eliminated. The latest group to return consisted of 180 residents of Guoba village in Sale township, who departed for home at around 6 pm Monday. The 444 returnees come from one village in Gyirong town and three villages in Sale township. Another 55 residents from a separate village in Gyirong town are preparing to return. The evacuation was prompted by a fast-moving chain mudslide triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal on Aug 26. The mudslide created a barrier lake above the core area of Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border, posing a serious threat to nearby villages. Local authorities relocated 499 residents from five villages in Gyirong town and Sale township to a temporary shelter. "We were well taken care of at the shelter, but I kept thinking about the livestock and crops back home," said Phurjung, a resident of Guoba village. Over the past several days, experts have conducted ongoing safety inspections and hydrological monitoring. The barrier lake above the main area of Gyirong Port has been drained, the river has resumed normal flow, and the risk has been largely removed. Local authorities checked the safety of houses and roads before arranging vehicles to transport residents home in batches. Upon returning to their villages, residents received food and other daily necessities delivered door to door by local officials. During the evacuation, local officials and village workers helped care for livestock, poultry and crops, and regularly shared video updates of the villages with residents at the shelter.

item.title: Changsha's stinky tofu draws crowds with its funky charm
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-09
Changsha's stinky tofu draws crowds with its funky charm Centuries-old snack assaults the nose, but conquers the taste buds The smell can be a bit overpowering, even off-putting. But one bite and you are hooked. That is the magic of stinky tofu in Changsha, Hunan province — a snack that has captivated locals and tourists alike for more than 200 years. "I grew up on this," said Shi Xukui, a 30-year-old office worker in Changsha. "It's not fancy. You stand by the cart, bite into it while it's piping hot, and the juice runs down your chin — that's the real taste of the city." Stinky tofu in Changsha is not just a snack — it's a dare, a comfort, a collective childhood memory and a daily delight. It assaults your nose way before it even reaches your lips: The aroma — pungent, earthy and deeply fermented — hits you from half a block away. However, the smell is only the opening act. Once the black cubes hit the sizzling oil at 150 C, they transform into a smoky, savory seduction that draws crowds like a magnet. Bite through the crackling shell, and a hot, spicy, garlic-laced broth explodes in your mouth — juicy, messy and utterly addictive. But here's the beauty of Changsha: No two batches of the delicacy taste exactly the same. At Fire God Palace (Huo Gong Dian) — a historic temple now turned into a time-honored dining destination known for traditional Hunan snacks — the brine is made from a secret family recipe and aged for two years. At Hey Hey Black, which has outlets everywhere, the seasoning packs a stronger punch with a chili kick that wakes up your palate. Then there are the nameless corner stalls. Vendors set up their carts at dusk, offering a comforting escape for workers and students weary after a whole day's labor. At about 2 yuan (30 US cents) a pop, it's an affordable thrill that appeals to all ages and income groups. The craft of making Fire God Palace stinky tofu has been recognized as a national intangible cultural heritage, said Zhou Houmu, a fourth-generation inheritor at Fire God Palace, who has been making it for over 17 years. Zhou said the process involves five steps: selecting the brine ingredients, making the brine, preparing the tofu curd, soaking the curd in the brine and deep-frying it. The brine is the heart of it all — a blend of more than 20 ingredients, including mushrooms, winter bamboo shoots, black fermented soybeans and perilla leaves. It ferments naturally for 18 months to two years, he said. "It's the brine that makes all the difference," Zhou said. "That's why our stinky tofu smells funky but tastes delicious." The proof lies in the eating. Liu Fei, 60, a visitor from Hebei province who grew up in Changsha, returned to the city recently with his family to revisit his childhood memories. "I've had stinky tofu in other places, but none of them compare to this," he said. "This is the most authentic you can get." Damon Shelby, a 27-year-old from the United States who is visiting Changsha, was equally smitten. "My first impression was that it was really moist, with lots of flavor all at once," he said. "I liked how juicy it was. It's interesting that it's black — we don't have anything like this in America. I feel it's really good to eat while you're walking." Long Shixing, head of operations at Fire God Palace, said the outlet sells about 4 million pieces of stinky tofu each year and has drawn over 7.22 million visitors so far this year. The rush typically peaks between 4 pm and 9 pm, when Changsha's vibrant nightlife comes alive, he said. Stinky tofu has become a signature of Changsha's food culture, said Zhou, the inheritor. "When you go out for a late-night snack in Changsha, you have to order a portion. It's like you haven't really been to Changsha if you haven't tried it."

item.title: Neighbors give Lao hospitals healthy dose of support
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-09
Neighbors give Lao hospitals healthy dose of support Cross-border care, training and medical exchanges boost patients' treatment options Laoportor, 42, recently crossed the border from Laos into southwestern China's Yunnan province for medical treatment after local doctors failed to resolve his health problems. The resident of a northern province of Laos was treated at a local hospital for several days for bile duct stones and liver-related issues. But his condition showed little improvement. On the advice of a Lao doctor, he traveled to Mengla County People's Hospital in Xishuangbanna Dai autonomous prefecture for further treatment. After spending a day and a night at the hospital, Laoportor said he felt much better. When interviewed by China Daily recently, he was still weak and remained in bed with his wife at his side. He said he was gradually recovering. "I am very grateful to the medical team here," he said. "The service and facilities are good, and the medical team is highly skilled. When I go back, I will recommend the hospital to people I know." Laoportor is far from alone. Xishuangbanna shares a 677-kilometer border with Laos. Six townships and 14 villages lie along the frontier. Mengla County People's Hospital received more than 13,000 foreign patients in 2025, compared with about 500 in 2013, according to Miao Zhihai, Party secretary of the hospital. Lao nationals accounted for 97.5 percent of its foreign patients last year. What began largely with emergency and critical cases has expanded to include chronic disease treatment, maternal and child healthcare, health checks and disease prevention, Miao said. Across Xishuangbanna, public medical institutions treated more than 30,000 foreign patients in 2025, according to the prefecture's health commission. But the growing flow of patients into China tells only part of the story. Along the border, Chinese medical services and expertise are being extended into Laos so more patients can be treated closer to home. However, this raises a practical question: can cross-border healthcare grow without putting pressure on Chinese medical resources? Hospital officials told China Daily the current number of foreign patients remains within the hospital system's capacity without affecting services for local residents.
